column1: [Foundation] What is byte-pair encoding, and why does the janitor's tokenizer start from the 256 bytes?
column2: Byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary by **merging the most frequent adjacent pair** into a new symbol, over and over; the merges, in the order they were learned, are the tokenizer. Starting from the **256 single bytes** means any text encodes with **no unknown token**. The price: a character outside ASCII is several tokens, as the é in café is two UTF-8 bytes.\n**A strong answer** calls the merge order part of the tokenizer, not just the vocabulary. (§From tokens to a distribution)

column1: [Foundation] What does the pre-tokenizer guarantee, and what does it mean for a resource id like vm-db-prod?
column2: The text is first cut by a regular expression into words, numbers, punctuation runs and whitespace, each taking at most one leading space, and **no token crosses a piece boundary**. So vm-db-prod becomes vm, -, db, -, prod before any merge applies: it is **five tokens however many merges you add**, and a pattern over tokens never sees the id whole.\n**A strong answer** blames the pre-tokenizer, not the size of the merge table. (§Tokenize)

column1: [Foundation] What are logits, and why are both the prompt and the reply length cost drivers?
column2: Logits are the scores one **forward pass** ends in, one per vocabulary token: the dot product of the last position's **hidden state** with that token's row of the output matrix. A pass scores only the next token, so a reply of n tokens takes **n forward passes**, and every pass reads the whole prompt again.\n**A strong answer** names the dot product: the nondeterminism story depends on it being a long sum. (§From tokens to a distribution)

column1: [Foundation] What does temperature change, and what can it never change?
column2: Dividing the logits by T below 1 widens their gaps, so the top token takes more of the mass; T above 1 flattens the distribution. Because exp is increasing and T is positive, **order is preserved**: temperature never changes which token is most likely. As T goes to 0 all mass goes to the argmax (**greedy decoding**); as T grows the distribution approaches uniform, and a logit of minus infinity stays at probability 0.\n**A strong answer** doesn't confuse a sharper distribution with a different top choice. (§From tokens to a distribution)

column1: [Foundation] What is nucleus (top-p) sampling, and how does it differ from top-k?
column2: Nucleus sampling keeps the **shortest prefix** of tokens, in decreasing probability, whose mass is **at least top_p**, renormalizes and draws from it. Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. A fixed k is wrong when the distribution is flat at one step and peaked at the next; the nucleus **adapts its size** to the distribution.\nTop-k and the nucleus answer different questions: a fixed number of tokens, or a fixed share of the mass. (§From tokens to a distribution)

column1: [Foundation] What is pass^k, and why does an agent that acts need it rather than pass@k?
column2: pass@k is the chance that **at least one** of k samples succeeds, the right question when a person picks the best try. **pass^k** is the chance that **all k** independent trials succeed, averaged over tasks. An agent acts on every run, so it needs the second. For the janitor a task is one candidate and success is agreeing with the greedy verdict: a low pass^k means its decision is a coin flip from run to run.\n**A strong answer** doesn't swap the two. (§From tokens to a distribution)

column1: [Foundation] What does "record, don't re-sample" mean, and why does the harness need it?
column2: A served model **isn't deterministic, even at temperature 0**, so to reproduce a run's model decisions the harness keeps the **raw text** the model wrote, with the **model binding and the date**, and replays it through the same parser instead of calling the model again. A run is evidence only if it can be examined again exactly.\n**A strong answer** says "the same parser": a recording replayed through a changed parser can give other decisions. (§Spec, model boundary: raw-output)

column1: [Foundation] What does ReplayModel guarantee when a call doesn't match its recorded line?
column2: It answers **every candidate SKIP** with the thesis that no recorded call matches: replay **fails closed** and never re-samples. Call i is answered from line i only, matched on the candidate ids in order and the **prompt hash**, and the replay moves to the next line on every call, matched or not. A replay that quietly called the model would be a new sample presented as a reproduction.\n**A strong answer** never searches the recording for another matching line. (§Spec, model boundary: replay)

column1: [Foundation] What is forced text in ToyLM, and why does it matter for the seed?
column2: Every reply position except the verdict has probability 1 and is **encoded with no draw**, so a reply about n candidates makes **exactly n draws**. That fixes the seed's meaning: the i-th draw always answers the i-th candidate, however long the JSON around it is. At the verdict row ARM scores a hand-set function of the evidence, SKIP scores 0, and every other token scores minus 12.\nThe trade-off: every factor is visible, but a real model computes a distribution at every position and can go wrong in the JSON too. (§Spec, model boundary: toylm)

column1: [Foundation] A sampled model armed ip-old-lb, which is tagged keep. What stopped it, and where do you see that?
column2: The **protected-tag gate (G1)** stopped it: the gates record for its delete shows allowed false with G1's reason. **The model proposes, code disposes**, for a sampled model exactly as for a rule-based one, because the gates sit after the model and judge whatever it proposes.\n**A strong answer** names the record that shows it, not just the gate. (§Generation)

column1: [Core] Implement encode for the janitor's BPE: pre-tokenize, then merge by rank inside each piece.
[Core] A teammate's encoder joins the leftmost adjacent pair that appears in the merge table. It matches yours on vm-db-prod. What's your review comment?
column2:
It must join the **lowest-ranked** pair, because **encoding replays training**: merge 0 was learned first, merge 1 on the result, and so on. Joining the leftmost listed pair gives ids the model never saw for that text. On short pieces the two rules often agree, which is why vm-db-prod passes; on longer ones they don't.
- **Fix:** take the minimum over (rank, position), so position decides only between equal ranks.
- **Test:** compare with frozen ids on longer strings, not only short ids.
**A strong answer** explains why order matters, not just stating the rule. (§Tokenize)

column1: [Core] Why are ARM after a quote and ARM with a leading space different token ids, and why does that matter to the parser?
column2: The leading space belongs to the pre-token, so ARM with a leading space is its own piece with its own merge, **token 411**, while ARM after a quote is **token 284**. The model writes whichever its distribution favors at that position, and only one of them is the verdict the parser accepts: the exact string ARM in the JSON verdict field. DISARM even ends in the token ARM.\n**A strong answer** says **a token is not a word**. (§Tokenize)

column1: [Core] Implement temperature-scaled softmax so that it never overflows.
column2:
Subtract the maximum logit before exponentiating, since softmax is unchanged when every logit shifts by the same constant.
```python
def softmax(z, T=1.0):
    if T < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"temperature must be >= 0, not {T}")
    m = max(z)
    if T == 0:  # greedy: one-hot at the first maximum
        i = z.index(m)
        return [1.0 if j == i else 0.0 for j in range(len(z))]
    e = [math.exp((x - m) / T) for x in z]  # largest term is exp(0) = 1
    s = sum(e)
    return [x / s for x in e]
```
The largest term is exp(0) = 1, so nothing overflows and the sum is at least 1, so nothing divides by zero; a logit of minus infinity gets exactly 0. This is the **log-sum-exp trick**.
**A strong answer** names the T = 0 branch and that `softmax([1000, 999])` doesn't raise `OverflowError`. (§Distributions)

column1: [Core] Implement top_p exactly as the sampling clause defines it.
column2:
Walk the entries in decreasing probability and stop at the first prefix whose running sum reaches top_p.
```python
def top_p(p, top_p):
    if not 0 < top_p <= 1:
        raise ValueError(f"top_p must be in (0, 1], not {top_p}")
    keep, mass = [], 0.0
    for i in _order(p):  # most probable first, ties to the lower index
        if p[i] == 0.0:
            break  # never keep an entry of probability 0
        keep.append(i)
        mass += p[i]
        if mass >= top_p:  # at least top_p, as computed
            break
    return _renormalize(p, keep)
```
Three details decide it: stop at `>=`, not `>`; compare the **running float sum** with no tolerance; never keep a zero. On [0.5, 0.25, 0.25] at 0.75 it keeps two; on [0.6, 0.3, 0.1] at 0.9 it keeps three, since 0.6 + 0.3 is 0.8999999999999999.
**A strong answer** names the **boundary**. (§Spec, model boundary: sampling)

column1: [Core] A teammate's nucleus compares mass >= top_p - 1e-9, "to be safe with floats." What's your review comment?
column2: Reject it: the sampling clause pins **mass >= top_p as computed, with no tolerance**, so that every conforming sampler keeps the same set. Most decimals aren't exact in binary, so the running sum lands a last bit above or below; a tolerance looks safer and **changes the set**. On [0.6, 0.3, 0.1] at 0.9 the clause keeps all three, because as doubles 0.6 + 0.3 is 0.8999999999999999; the tolerance keeps two.\n**A strong answer** treats the boundary as specified behavior, not a float bug to smooth over. (§Spec, model boundary: sampling)

column1: [Core] Logits are ARM 2.0, SKIP 1.6, other 0. Why does temperature 0.1 still sometimes draw SKIP, and which settings would make it never do so?
column2: At T = 0.1 the gap of 0.4 becomes 4, and exp(-4) leaves SKIP about **1.8% of the mass**: 174 of 10,000 draws at seed 7. A low temperature makes the second choice **rare, not impossible**. Only a setting that removes SKIP from the set the draw is made from makes it 0: T = 0, top_k = 1, or a top_p no larger than P(ARM) at that temperature, about 0.982.\n**A strong answer** doesn't call a low temperature greedy. (§From tokens to a distribution)

column1: [Core] Can temperature change the nucleus, and what happens when you set both top_k and top_p?
column2: Yes: temperature keeps the order, so never the top token, but it changes the probabilities and so **how many tokens it takes to reach top_p**; on the lab's verdict row the nucleus at 0.9 grows from two tokens to four as T rises. With both cuts the sampler applies **softmax, then top-k, then the nucleus**, then exactly one draw. The order matters: on a hot row the nucleus of the top two can be one token where the top two of the nucleus are two.\n**A strong answer** treats the order as part of the sampler's definition. (§Distributions)

column1: [Core] A teammate makes SampledModel create random.Random(seed) inside every decide call, "so each call is reproducible." What breaks?
column2: Every call **repeats the same first draws**, so two calls about the same candidate always agree and K calls measure one draw K times. The model must hold **one generator for its lifetime**, so each call draws where the last one stopped. The bug is easy to miss because the result is still reproducible: it reproducibly measures the same draw.\n**A strong answer** separates reproducible from independent: the seed fixes the whole sequence, and the order of calls fixes which draw answers which candidate. (§Generation)

column1: [Core] Implement the pass^k estimator for a task with n trials, c of them successes.
column2:
Count the k-subsets of the n trials that are all successes.
```python
def pass_k(n, c, k):
    if not (1 <= k <= n and 0 <= c <= n):
        raise ValueError(f"need 1 <= k <= n and 0 <= c <= n, not n={n} c={c} k={k}")
    return math.comb(c, k) / math.comb(n, k)  # 0 when c < k
```
C(c, k) / C(n, k) is the chance that k trials chosen **without replacement** are all successes, and its average over every outcome is exactly q to the k. The plug-in (c / n) to the k samples with replacement and, by **Jensen's inequality**, overestimates for every k of 2 or more.
**A strong answer** names the bias direction. (§Measure, record, replay)

column1: [Core] Why doesn't pinning the sampler's seed or setting temperature 0 make a served model reproducible?
column2: Both fix only the sampler; neither fixes the **logits** the draws come from. **Floating-point addition isn't associative**, GPU kernels split their reductions by **batch size**, and the batch depends on how many other requests the server is handling, so a near-tie can flip between calls. The near-tie lab shows it at T = 0 with no random number: one 4,096-term dot product summed sequentially, pairwise and blocked(128) gives three values of each logit, and the verdicts disagree.\n**A strong answer** locates the cause in the server's arithmetic, not the sampler. (§Make it deterministic)

column1: [Core] A teammate caches replies keyed by a hash of the whole prompt, so next week's call agrees with today's. What's your review comment?
column2:
The second call agrees only because **it isn't a call**: it is replay under another name. Any change in the evidence, a new tag or one more idle day, misses the cache and makes a **fresh call that can disagree**, so the cache doesn't fix nondeterminism.
- **Keep:** recording the raw output, as a recording.
- **Measure:** how often fresh calls disagree, with pass^k.
- **Rely on:** the gates after the model, so a verdict that goes the other way is still safe.
**A strong answer** says nothing the janitor does alone makes two fresh calls agree. (§Make it deterministic)

column1: [Core] Why did the substring matcher arm replies that said no, and why is .strip().upper() the wrong fix?
column2:
It armed whenever the text ARM appeared in the candidate's object: inside DISARM and WARM in a thesis, and inside a DISARM verdict, so **a string match on the verdict fails open**. Normalizing with .strip().upper() makes ARM with a leading space and Arm arm: tokens the model wrote that the protocol doesn't allow.
- **Fix:** decode the JSON array and compare the verdict field with == "ARM".
- **Not a fix:** "ARM" in verdict, which still arms FARM.
- **Not a fix:** a regex for the verdict near the id, which arms a SKIP whose meta object says "verdict": "ARM".
**A strong answer** reads the field, **exactly**. (§Break it: string matching)

column1: [Core] A CLIModel call fails with "Your credit balance is too low.", which the unavailable pattern doesn't match. What happens, and is that a safety or an availability problem?
column2: The failure is treated as a **real error**: CLIModel stops without trying the next model and returns every candidate SKIP, so nothing is deleted and the run is a day without cleanup. That is an **availability cost, not a safety defect**, and the asymmetry is designed. The open direction is a **false match**: prose that says "quota" or "429" about something else moves the call to a lower-ranked model, and only the recording's binding shows it.\n**A strong answer** names both directions of the matcher. (§Break it: string matching)

column1: [Advanced] You retrain the janitor's merge table from its corpus with your own trainer. The first merges match the shipped table and later ids don't. What happened, and why must a tokenizer be reproducible byte for byte?
column2:
Most likely your trainer broke a **tie between equally frequent pairs** differently. Sennrich et al.'s Algorithm 1 gives no tie rule, so the choice falls to dictionary iteration order, and **every id after the first tie shifts**. That matters because a tokenizer is **data the model was trained against**: the toy finds its verdict tokens by these ids, and the table must not change once oracles are recorded against it.
- **Plan:** fix one explicit tie rule and reproduce the shipped table exactly from the corpus with 200 merges.
- **Verify:** compare ids on frozen strings, not token counts.
**A strong answer** treats the tie rule as part of the tokenizer. (§Problem set)

column1: [Advanced] You're moving the janitor from ToyLM to a served model with its own tokenizer. The janitor still runs and the parser still passes its tests. What doesn't carry over, and what goes into the plan?
column2:
Anything counted in tokens and every number measured on the toy. **Tokenizers are model-specific**, so token counts, context limits and prices don't transfer, and the toy's probabilities were known exactly where a real model's are not.
- **Budgets:** recount prompt and reply tokens with the new tokenizer.
- **Failure surface:** a real reply can change the JSON layout, skip or repeat a candidate, or add prose; the parser must take it.
- **Evidence:** record the binding, the date and the raw text, since the served model isn't deterministic.
- **Measurement:** estimate disagreement and pass^k from a recording.
The trade-off: the toy made every factor visible; the served model shows only text, so the recording becomes the evidence. (§Optional: a real model)

column1: [Advanced] A teammate proposes calling the model five times per run and acting on the majority. disk-scratch-7 has P(ARM) of about 0.524. Evaluate the proposal.
column2:
It barely helps: with q = 0.524 the majority of five disagrees with the greedy verdict when at most two agree, about **0.45**, against one call's 0.48. **A near-tie stays a near-tie**; voting helps only where the model is already fairly sure, and there it isn't needed.
- **Independence:** five calls can land on the same servers under the same load, so their errors can be **correlated**, and then the majority is wrong more often than the binomial says.
- **Cost:** five times the tokens and latency per run.
- **Replay:** all five samples must be recorded for the run to be replayed.
**A strong answer** computes it instead of assuming that averaging helps. (§Problem set)

column1: [Advanced] Your task is to make next week's fresh call to the served model give today's verdicts. A teammate proposes temperature 0, a pinned seed and sending each request alone. What do you tell them, and what do you build instead?
column2:
None of them makes two fresh calls agree. **Temperature 0** removes only the sampler's randomness; a **pinned seed** fixes the draws, not the logits, which depend on the batch the request shared; and the server batches every client's requests, so "alone" isn't the client's choice. **Batch-invariant kernels** remove the batch dependence at a cost in throughput, but only the server's operator can deploy them.
- **Record:** raw text, binding and date, replayed through the same parser.
- **Measure:** disagreement and pass^k.
- **Gate:** keep the gates after the model.
**A strong answer** accepts that a harness can't make a served model deterministic. (§Make it deterministic)

column1: [Advanced] An auditor replays yesterday's recording and gets different decisions from the ledger. What could cause it, and what does a replay not reproduce even when it matches?
column2: Either the recording isn't the one the run made, such as another file or a run that called the model twice, or the replay's call isn't the recorded call: other candidates because the inventory changed, or another context. ReplayModel detects the second and answers **all SKIP**. A recording also names no parser version, so a **changed parser** can give other decisions. Even a matching replay reproduces **only the model's side**: the gates still read the clock, HALT, the mode and the inventory.\n**A strong answer** separates reproducing the model's decisions from reproducing the whole run. (§Measure, record, replay)

column1: [Advanced] A teammate wants ReplayModel to match on candidate ids alone and to search the recording for any line with those ids, "so a replay survives reordering." What's your review comment?
column2:
Both changes replay **an answer to a different question**. The same candidates with another owner note, a new keep tag or another idle count are a different call, which is why the **prompt hash** of the whole prompt is in the match. And a run whose calls come in another order **isn't the recorded run**; answering SKIP says so.
- **Match:** candidate ids in order, and the prompt hash.
- **Advance:** move to the next line on every call, matched or not.
- **On a miss:** answer every candidate SKIP and never call a model.
The trade-off: a strict replay misses more often, but every miss is a SKIP that acts on nothing. (§Spec, model boundary: replay)

column1: [Advanced] A sampler draws at T = 0.8 when asked for 0.7, and the three-standard-error measurement check passes. What does that say about your test strategy?
column2:
The statistical check is the wrong tool for that bug: a **consistency check at three standard errors** has little power against a sampler that is only a little wrong, and this one passes 196 of the stress run's 200 seeds. What catches it is the **exact generation tests** that rebuild every draw. The statistical check is for what exact tests can't reach: whether the measurement, end to end, agrees with the probabilities it claims to measure.
- **Exact tests:** pin the sampler's arithmetic, draw for draw.
- **Statistical check:** about 1 seed in 230 fails a correct implementation, always the same ones.
**A strong answer** knows what each kind of test can see. (§Measure, record, replay)

column1: [Advanced] An incident review finds the old substring matcher armed bucket-tmp because a thesis said "WARM standby". What do you change, and what does the fix still not guarantee?
column2:
Replace the matcher with the **strict parser rule**: decode the JSON, accept an answer only when its candidate_id is known and its verdict is exactly "ARM" or "SKIP", default everything else to **SKIP**, and never raise. The gates are no backstop here: nothing stops a bucket-tmp armed by a word if its gates pass, and **the parser is the only part that knows what the model said**.
- **Test:** FARM, ARM with a leading space, Arm, ARMED, a list verdict, a nested verdict field, a reply that isn't JSON.
- **Still open:** how the array is found; each choice has a weakness on some malformed reply.
**A strong answer** names what the fix leaves open. (§Break it: string matching)
